stem: Which Gupta ruler assumed the throne after killing his elder brother?

options.label: e
options.text: None of the above/More than one of the above

expl: After Samudragupta, his son Ramagupta became the ruler. However, since he could not effectively resist the Shaka invasions, his brother Chandragupta II killed Ramagupta, married his wife Dhruvadevi, and achieved victory over the Shakas.

stem: Who is called ‘the Napoleon of Ancient India’?
expl: Historian Vincent Smith, impressed by Samudragupta’s valour and conquests, gave him the title ‘Indian Napoleon’ in his work The Early History of India. Samudragupta’s conquests are described in the Prayag-Prashasti. Its author was Harishena.

stem: The Gupta emperor who defeated the ‘Hunas’ was:
expl: The first Huna invasion of India took place during the reign of the Gupta emperor Skandagupta (around 455 CE), and they were badly defeated by him. This invasion was only a raid and had no major direct impact on the country; however, indirectly it accelerated the decline of the Gupta Empire. After Skandagupta’s death, in the late 5th century and the beginning of the 6th century, the Hunas captured several regions in the north-west.

stem: Who was the founder of Nalanda University?
expl: According to Hiuen Tsang, the founder of Nalanda University was ‘Shakraditya’, who established it due to his great devotion to Buddhism. Shakraditya is identified with the Gupta ruler Kumaragupta I (415–455 CE). Kumaragupta’s famous title was ‘Mahendraditya’. Nalanda was a renowned Buddhist centre and university. It was located near Rajgir in southern Bihar. Even today, its ruins are scattered far and wide around the village of Bargaon. In the mid-5th century, during the Gupta period, Nalanda University came into existence. Kumaragupta I was the first to donate to the Nalanda Buddhist Vihara, and later Gupta rulers such as Buddhagupta and Baladitya also

stem: Why was Nalanda University famous in the world?
expl: Nalanda University was world-famous for the study of Buddhist philosophy. The Chinese traveller Hiuen Tsang came to India to study there.

stem:
Out of two statements below first is Assertion(A) and second is Reason (R), carefully read both statements.
Assertion (A) : Till the end of the twelfth century Nalanda Mahavihara lost its glory.
Reason (R) : State protection ceased to be available to the Mahavihara. With respect to the above-mentioned two statements, which of the following is true?

options.label: a
options.text: (A) and (R) both are true, and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).

options.label: b
options.text: (A) and (R) both are true, and (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).

expl: Nalanda was a renowned Buddhist centre and university. It was located near Rajgir (ancient name: Rajgriha) in southern Bihar. The university at Nalanda came into existence in the mid-5th century during the time of the Gupta rulers. In the last decade of the 12th century, as a result of Muslim invasions, this Mahavihara declined. Also, because the Pala rulers of Bengal patronised Vikramashila University, the importance of Nalanda began to diminish.

stem:
Consider the following statements :
1. Fa-Hien was a Chinese pilgrim who visited India during the reign of Harsha.
2. Hiuen Tsang was a Chinese Buddhist monk who visited India during the reign of Chandragupta II.
Which of the above statements is/are correct?
expl: Fa-Hien was a Chinese traveler, and he visited India during the reign of Chandragupta II. He wrote a detailed account of the life of the people here. In his account, he did not mention the king’s name. The Chinese traveler Hiuen Tsang visited India during the reign of Emperor Harsha. He described the multi-storeyed bronze monastery built by Harsha at Nalanda. In his account, he mentioned that during Harsha’s period the Shudras practiced agriculture. He also mentioned the assembly held at Prayagraj (Prayag) in his travelogue. Therefore, both statement (1) and statement (2) are incorrect.

stem: The gradual decline of towns was an important feature of which period?
expl: In the Gupta period, towns moved towards gradual decline. Across the entire Ganga valley, many cities that were earlier extremely prosperous were either abandoned in the Gupta age or witnessed considerable disruption in settlement. By the time of Xuanzang’s arrival, even an important city like Pataliputra had turned into a village. Important towns like Mathura, and places such as Kumhrar, Sonpur, Sohgaura, and many significant centers of the Ganga valley in Uttar Pradesh also show clear evidence of decline.

stem: Which one of the following ports was in use for the North Indian trade during the Gupta period?

options.label: e
options.text: None of the above/More than one of the above

expl: During the Gupta period, Tamralipti in Bengal was a major port, from where North India traded with South-East Asia, China, Lanka, Java, Sumatra, etc. The major port of western India was Bhrigukachchha (Bharuch), from where maritime trade took place with western countries. Besides this, Kalyan and Cambay were also used for North Indian trade.

stem: Which ruling dynasty donated the maximum villages to temples and Brahmins?
expl: The rulers of the Gupta dynasty gave the maximum number of village grants to temples and Brahmins. The land grants mentioned in Gupta inscriptions make it clear that along with the land grant, the income generated from the village land was also handed over to the recipient.

stem: What was the land revenue rate in the Gupta age?
expl: In the Gupta period, those who cultivated on state land had to pay a part of their produce (one-sixth of the produce) to the king as tax, which was called Shashthansh (one-sixth). In Gupta inscriptions, this land tax is referred to as ‘Bhagkar’ or ‘Udrang’.

stem: What is the rate of land revenue in the Dharmashastras?
expl: In almost all Dharmashastra texts, the rate of land revenue was 1/6 (one-sixth of the produce).

stem: What type of land was called ‘Aprahata’?

options.label: e
options.text: None of the above / More than one of the above

expl: Unploughed wild land (land on which cultivation has not been done) was called ‘Aprahata land’. This is a term of the Gupta-period revenue system.

stem:
Consider the types of land according to the Amarkosha:
(A) Urvara-fertile
(B) Maru-desert
(C) Shadvala-grassy
(D) Devamatrika-watered by rain
Which of the following is correct ?

options.label: d
options.text: More than one of the above

expl: Amara Singh one of the Navaratnas (nine gems) of Chandragupta II ‘Vikramaditya’, composed the work titled ‘Amarakosha’. Amarakosha gives a list of 12 types of land, including—Urvara (fertile land), Maru (desert land), Ushara (barren land), Aprahata (fallow land), Shadvala/Shadbala (grass land), Pankila (muddy land), Jalaprayanupama (moist land), Kaccha (marshy land/land near water sources), Sharkara (limestone/pebble-bearing land), Sharkaravati (sandy land), Nadimatrika (river-irrigated land) and Devamatrika (rain-fed). Hence, all the matchings given in the options are correct. Therefore, option (d) is the correct answer.

stem: Who was the author of the famous ‘Allahabad Prashasti’?

options.label: e
options.text: None of the above / More than one of the above

expl: The author of the famous Allahabad Prashasti was Harishena. On the Ashokan pillar at Allahabad (present-day Prayagraj), Harishena presented a eulogistic account of Samudragupta, which is called the ‘Prayag Prashasti’. In the same Prashasti, Harishena described himself as Sandhivigrahika, Kumaramatya and Dandanayaka. This implies that in the Gupta period, a person could be appointed to more than one post.

stem: In the Puranas, the rulers of which dynasty were called ‘Shriparvatiya’?
expl: In the Puranas, the rulers of the Ikshvaku dynasty are called ‘Shriparvatiya’ (rulers of the Shriparvata region) and ‘Andhrabhritya’ (servants of the Andhras). Earlier, they were feudatories of the Satavahanas, but after their decline they declared independence. The founder of this dynasty was Shri Shantamula.

stem:
Consider the following about the King “Pravaerasena” :
(A) He was the real founder of the Vakataka dynasty.
(B) His empire extended from Bundelkhand in the north to Hyderabad in the South.
(C) He succeeded his father king Vindhyashakti.
(D) He is mentioned in the Puranas.
Which of the following statements are correct ?

options.label: d
options.text: More than one of the above

expl: The Vakataka dynasty was an ancient Indian dynasty that ruled the central and southern parts of India from the 3rd century CE to the end of the 5th century CE / beginning of the 6th century CE. The founder of this dynasty was Vindhyashakti I, whose successor was Pravarasena I, who is also called the real founder of the Vakataka dynasty. During the time of Pravarasena I, the boundaries of the Vakataka kingdom expanded from the Vindhya region in the north (the present Bundelkhand region is included in this) to the Deccan in the south (present Hyderabad also fell within his sphere of influence). Among the Vakataka rulers, he was the first to assume the title of ‘Samrat’ and performed four Ashvamedha sacrifices and other Vedic rituals. In the Puranas, he is referred to as ‘Praveera’. Hence, all four statements are true.

stem: The Huna King Toramana was defeated by the Aulikara King

options.label: e
options.text: None of the above/More than one of the above

expl: The Huna king Toramana was defeated by the Aulikara king Prakashadharman. After the death of Skandagupta, the Hunas again attacked the Ganga valley. The leader of this second Huna invasion was Toramana. His inscription has been found engraved on a Varaha (boar) image at Eran in Central India. Two seals of Toramana have been found at Kaushambi. Toramana appointed his son Mihirakula as his successor.

stem: Who laid the foundation of the Vardhana Dynasty?

options.label: e
options.text: None of the above/More than one of the above

expl: According to Banabhatta’s work Harshacharita, the Vardhana dynasty was founded by a person named Pushyabhuti at Thaneshwar/Sthaneshwar. Harshavardhana was the greatest ruler of this dynasty.

stem: Poet Bana was an inhabitant of –
expl: There is considerable disagreement among scholars regarding the birthplace of Banabhatta. According to some scholars, he was born in a village named Pritikuta located on the bank of the Son River in Bihar, while others believe he was born in a village named Pritikut near Kanyakubja (Kannauj) in Uttar Pradesh. His father’s name was Chitrabhanu and his mother’s name was Rajadevi.

stem: Which Chinese traveller visited India during Harshavardhana’s rule?
expl: The most important event of Harshavardhana’s time was the arrival of the Chinese traveller Hiuen Tsang in India. His strong desire was to see the places made sacred by the footprints of Gautama Buddha and to study the sacred Buddhist texts, which were available in India in those days. To fulfil this aim, he left Chang'an (Changan), the capital of the Tang rulers, for India in 629 CE. He wrote a book about his Indian journey, known as Si-Yu-Ki.

stem: Chinese traveller Hiuen Tsang studied at the University of –
expl: In 637 CE, Hiuen Tsang went to Nalanda University. At that time, the Vice-Chancellor there was Acharya Shilabhadra. He stayed at Nalanda for about 15 months and studied Yogashastra under Acharya Shilabhadra. After this, he reached Kanchi via Bengal, Odisha and Dhanyakataka. In the second phase of his journey, Hiuen Tsang again came to Nalanda in 642 CE. Thus, the total period of his stay at Nalanda (combining both visits) was about two years.

stem: During Hiuen-Tsang tour in India the most famous city for the production of cotton clothes was:
expl: The Chinese traveller Hiuen Tsang came to India during the time of Harshavardhana (606–647 CE). According to him, Mathura was famous for cotton textiles at that time, whereas Varanasi was famous for silk textiles. He also states that the main reason for the prosperity of Thaneshwar was trade. Bana described the city of Thaneshwar as a “land of wish-fulfilment” for guests and a “red land” for merchants. Most of its inhabitants were traders who dealt in various goods. Ujjayini and Kannauj were also very prosperous economically during this period.

stem: Which of the following rulers ruled Assam during the time of Harsha?

options.label: d
options.text: More than one of the above

expl: Among the given options, during Harsha’s time, Bhaskar Varman ruled Assam. Bhaskar Varman was a ruler of the Varman dynasty in Kamarupa (Assam). According to Mukunda Madhava Sharma’s book 'Inscription of Ancient Assam' and the Assam Gazetteer, after Bhaskar Varman, for a few years Avanti Varman became the ruler; Salastambha removed him from the throne and seized the throne.

stem: Who was the ruler of India during the 7th century CE known for his patronage of Buddhism and support for cultural activities?

options.label: d
options.text: More than one of the above

expl: During the 7th century AD, Harsha (Harshavardhana), a ruler of the Pushyabhuti dynasty, is known for patronizing Buddhism and supporting cultural activities. Harshavardhana ruled from about 606 AD to about 647 AD (about 41 years).

stem: During the Gupta-Vakataka Era, which important school of Indian philosophy developed, focusing on logical reasoning and debate?

options.label: d
options.text: More than one of the above

expl: In the Gupta–Vakataka age, the school of Indian philosophy that developed with a focus on logical reasoning and debate was Nyaya. The founder of Nyaya philosophy is Gautama. According to Nyaya, knowledge can be valid or invalid. Valid knowledge is called Prama, and invalid knowledge is called Aprama.

stem: Who among these was the first to explain that the daily sunrise and sunset occur due to the Earth's rotation on its axis?

options.label: e
options.text: None of the above/More than one of the above

expl: Aryabhatta was the first person to explain that the daily sunrise and sunset occur because the Earth rotates on its axis.

stem: Who among the following is known for his work on medicine during the Gupta period?

options.label: e
options.text: None of the above/More than one of the above

expl: Sushruta is called the “Father of Surgery.” He was from Kashi, and his period is generally considered to be about 1000 BC to 600 BC. Shaunaka was a sage of the Rigvedic period. Shudraka was a Gupta-period playwright. Saumila is a Gupta-period playwright, whom Kalidasa mentions along with Bhasa and Kaviputra. Thus, in the Gupta period, none of the above worked in the field of medicine. However, the Bihar Public Service Commission, in both its preliminary and final answer keys, considered option (a) as the correct answer. Since the Gupta period begins from 275 AD (Sri Gupta), which is about 1000 years after the accepted period of Sushruta (about 1000 BC to 600 BC), it is not reasonable to consider Sushruta as a contemporary of the Gupta period.
